title: There's a real physics paper called "Why the Brazil nuts are on top"
hook: Shake mixed nuts and the big ones rise. A 1987 physics paper dug into it

open.title: Scientists wrote a paper on why the heavy nut ends up on top when you shake
open.line: Shake a bag of mixed nuts and the biggest Brazil nut often ends up right on top.

summary: Shaken together, big pieces rise above small ones even if made of heavier stuff, a 1987 paper showed. A 2001 experiment found air pressure inside changes it too.

text: Shake a bag of mixed nuts and the biggest Brazil nut often lands on top.
In 1987, four researchers wrote a physics paper on it.
Its title really is "Why the Brazil nuts are on top."
It ran in the physics journal Physical Review Letters: 3 pages.
They shook a can over and over in a computer.
Bury coins at the bottom of a jar of rice, shake, and up they come.
Actually, the big ball rises even when it's denser than the small ones.
It isn't sifting, they noted, where small grains drop through gaps.
One idea: each shake, small bits slip into the gap under the big one.
Raisins piling atop a cereal bag are thought to be the same thing.
In a 2001 Nature experiment, the big piece's weight didn't push results one way.
Changing only the air pressure changed it too.

sources: Rosato et al., Why the Brazil nuts are on top, Phys. Rev. Lett. 58, 1038 (1987) abstract
Möbius et al., Size separation of granular particles, Nature 414, 270 (2001)
